message:
QUESTION:
Did guard X's three-point shooting genuinely improve after the mid-season change of shooting coach, and should X take a larger share of the team's three-point attempts next season?

DATA:
Professional basketball. Guard X's shooting before and after a mid-season change of shooting coach, which took effect after game 30. X played in all 50 games. His minutes per game were similar in both periods (about 32).

Shooting percentage = makes / attempts.

| | Games 1-30 | Games 31-50 |
| Three-point attempts | 150 | 80 |
| Three-point makes | 51 | 32 |
| Free-throw attempts | 100 | 70 |
| Free-throw makes | 80 | 55 |

League average three-point percentage this season: 36%.

Opponent breakdown: in games 31-50, 30 of X's 80 three-point attempts came in 4 games against the league's two worst-ranked perimeter defences, and he made 18 of those 30. X did not face either of those teams in games 1-30.

The coaching staff must decide whether to increase X's share of team three-point attempts next season. The new shooting coach worked with the whole squad, not just X.

<analysis>
# Receipt

**1. Remove the references to a draft (the most important fix).**
The "Main corrections to the draft" section and the line in Section 3 about "the draft cited… 86%" refer to a document the coaching staff has never seen. Both should go. Section 3 should simply state that free-throw percentage fell from 80.0% to 78.6%. Any change log belongs in a separate note.

**2. The shot-selection argument doesn't fit the split.**
The analysis suggested that taking fewer threes might have raised X's percentage through better shot selection. The split points the other way:
- Against the two weakest defences he took about 7.5 attempts per game and shot 60%.
- Against everyone else he took about 3.1 per game and shot 28%.

So the games with fewer, supposedly "more selective" shots were his worst. The point should be dropped or reframed. One reframing is that normal defences may have been limiting his looks. The claim that more volume next season would lower his efficiency should also be softened, because these data don't show it.

**3. Say whether 36.1% is a fair or flattering baseline.**
Excluding the 30 attempts against the weakest defences, X shot 65/200 = 32.5% for the season. The right planning figure depends on how often he will face weak defences next season. The analysis needs a sentence on this. Either figure still supports "no increase."

**4. Make the decision trigger concrete.**
"Clearly above league average" after 250–300 attempts needs a number. At about 275 attempts the standard error is about 2.9 points. The reviewer suggests roughly 40% or better. Rates of 37–38% would still be within noise. I checked this: a one-sided 95% threshold works out to about 41% (36 + 1.65 × 2.9). I use about 40–41% below.

**Minor points.**
- "Weak opponents explain the gain" is slightly too strong, because both sub-samples are small. "Is accounted for by" is more precise.
- Equal minutes rule out playing time as a cause. They don't fully rule out a minor injury, so that sentence should claim only that playing time doesn't explain the difference.

**What the review does not change:** every figure checks out, and the conclusion and recommendation stand. I also checked the reviewer's new numbers (32.5%, 2.9 pp, 7.5 and 3.1 attempts per game) and they are correct.

---

# Guard X: Three-Point Shooting Since the Coaching Change

## Summary

The data do not show that X's three-point shooting genuinely improved after the change of shooting coach. They do not support giving him a larger share of the team's three-point attempts next season.

His raw percentage rose from 34.0% to 40.0%, but three facts undercut that rise:

- **The gain is accounted for by weak opponents.** The rise comes entirely from 30 attempts against the league's two weakest perimeter defences, teams he did not face before game 30. Against all other opponents he shot 28% after the change, below his pre-change rate.
- **The gap is within normal variation.** Even before adjusting for opponents, a 6-point difference on these sample sizes is easily produced by chance.
- **Free throws did not improve.** His free-throw percentage fell slightly, from 80.0% to 78.6%. There is no corroborating sign of better mechanics.

The best current estimate of X's ability is somewhere between 32.5% and 36%. That is at or a little below league average.

## Data and context

- The season is split at game 30, when the new shooting coach took over. The coach works with the whole squad, not only X.
- X played all 50 games, at about 32 minutes per game in both periods. Changes in playing time therefore do not explain any difference.
- Shooting percentage = makes ÷ attempts.

| | Games 1–30 | Games 31–50 | Season |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three-point makes / attempts | 51 / 150 | 32 / 80 | 83 / 230 |
| Three-point % | 34.0% | 40.0% | 36.1% |
| Three-point attempts per game | 5.0 | 4.0 | 4.6 |
| Free-throw makes / attempts | 80 / 100 | 55 / 70 | 135 / 170 |
| Free-throw % | 80.0% | 78.6% | 79.4% |

League average three-point percentage: 36%.

## 1. The headline improvement is driven by opponents

In games 31–50, 30 of X's 80 attempts came in 4 games against the two worst-ranked perimeter defences. He made 18 of them. He did not play either team in games 1–30, so the two periods faced different opposition.

| Games 31–50 | Games | Makes / attempts | % | Attempts per game |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vs two worst perimeter defences | 4 | 18 / 30 | 60.0% | 7.5 |
| vs all other opponents | 16 | 14 / 50 | 28.0% | 3.1 |
| Total | 20 | 32 / 80 | 40.0% | 4.0 |

The "all other opponents" group is the one most comparable to his games 1–30 schedule. Against it X shot 28%, which is 6 points worse than before the change, not better.

The 60% figure rests on only 30 shots over 4 games. It should not be read as his true level against weak defences. Still, the split shows that the aggregate 40% reflects the schedule, not a better shooter.

## 2. Even the raw difference is within chance

Set the opponent split aside. A rise from 34.0% (150 attempts) to 40.0% (80 attempts) has a standard error of about 6.7 percentage points. The 6-point gain is therefore less than one standard error, well within what random variation produces.

A true 36% shooter would quite often post a 34% stretch followed by a 40% stretch over samples this size. Three-point percentage needs several hundred attempts to stabilise, and the post-change sample is 80.

The 28% figure against other opponents is just as noisy, on only 50 attempts. The honest conclusion is not that X got worse. It is that, once opponents are accounted for, nothing in these data distinguishes his shooting after the change from his shooting before it.

## 3. Free throws do not suggest a change in mechanics

X's free-throw percentage fell slightly, from 80.0% (80/100) to 78.6% (55/70). On 70 attempts that change is too small to mean anything.

Free throws are a reasonable, if imperfect, check on shooting technique, because they are uncontested and taken from a fixed spot. They give no sign of a mechanical improvement.

## 4. Other points to note

**Volume and opponents.** X's attempts fell from 5.0 to 4.0 per game at the same minutes. The split shows this was not a move toward fewer, better shots:
- Against the weakest defences he took 7.5 attempts per game and shot well.
- Against everyone else he took about 3.1 per game, down from 5.0 before the change, and shot 28%.

One possible reading is that normal defences were limiting his looks. These data cannot confirm that, and they say nothing about how his efficiency would change at higher volume.

**Which baseline to plan around.** His full-season rate is 36.1%. Without the 30 attempts against the two weakest defences, it is 32.5% (65/200).
- Four of 50 games against those teams may be a normal share of the schedule.
- However, those games produced 13% of his attempts, so they carry extra weight in the season figure.
- A planning range of roughly 32.5–36% is therefore reasonable.

Either end of that range is at or below league average.

**The coach worked with the whole squad.** The team's own before-and-after three-point figures, split by opponent strength, would be a far better test of the coaching effect than one player's 80 attempts.
- If the whole team improved against comparable opponents, that would be meaningful evidence.
- If only X's numbers rose, and only against weak defences, that points to the schedule and to chance.

**Expected value.** At 36.1%, an X three is worth about 1.08 points per attempt, the same as a league-average three. At 32.5% it is about 0.98. There is no evidence that moving attempts from teammates to X would add points. That depends on how teammates compare, which these data do not show.

## Recommendation

1. **Do not increase X's share of team three-point attempts on the strength of this data.** Plan around him as a roughly league-average or slightly below-average three-point shooter (about 32.5–36%).
2. **Run the comparison that would actually answer the question.** Compare opponent-adjusted three-point percentage before and after the change, for X and for the rest of the squad. Where tracking data exist, also compare shot quality: contested versus open, and catch-and-shoot versus off-the-dribble.
3. **Keep collecting evidence.** Continue X's work with the new coach. Reassess once he has a few hundred post-change attempts against a representative range of opponents.
4. **Set a concrete decision trigger in advance.** After about 250–300 further attempts, the standard error on his percentage will be about 2.9 points.
   - Revisit his role if his opponent-adjusted rate is about 40–41% or better. That is clearly above the 36% league average.
   - Do not act on a rate of 37–38%, because that is still within noise.
   - Do not reward or penalise him on short streaks in either direction.
</analysis>

Please review this analysis.
response:
# Review: Guard X Three-Point Analysis

**Verdict:** The figures are correct and the conclusion is sound. One structural fix is needed before this goes to the coaching staff, and a few points could be sharper.

## Figures checked

All of these are correct:

- **Three-point %:** 34.0%, 40.0% and 36.1% season (83/230).
- **Free-throw %:** 80.0%, 78.6% and 79.4%.
- **Attempts per game:** 5.0, 4.0 and 4.6. In the split, 7.5 and 3.125 (shown as 3.1).
- **Split percentages:** 60% (18/30) and 28% (14/50).
- **Season excluding weak defences:** 32.5% (65/200).
- **Share of attempts against weak defences:** 13% (30/230).
- **Standard error of the 34% vs 40% difference:** √(.34·.66/150 + .40·.60/80) ≈ 6.7 points.
- **Standard error at 275 attempts and 36%:** ≈ 2.9 points. The one-sided 95% threshold is 36 + 1.645 × 2.9 ≈ 40.8%.
- **Points per attempt:** 1.08 at 36.1% and 0.98 at 32.5%.

## Must fix

**1. Remove the "Receipt" section from the deliverable.**
Its own point 1 says references to a draft should go. Yet the whole Receipt is a change log about a draft and a reviewer the staff have never seen. It also contains working notes such as "I checked this" and "I use about 40–41% below." Send it as a separate note to whoever requested the revision, or delete it. The report should start at the title.

## Should consider

**2. The 32.5% lower bound is biased downward.**
Removing only the two worst defences strips out the easiest part of his schedule. It leaves in every other below-average defence, and every real schedule includes weak teams. The 36.1% season figure, with 4 of 50 games against those teams, may well be close to a normal schedule.

There is also a reason to expect his true rate is near 36%. With only 230 attempts, a sensible estimate of his ability shifts strongly toward the league average.

I suggest framing 32.5% as a conservative floor rather than an equally likely end of the range. Say his best estimate is roughly league average, about 35–36%. The recommendation does not change.

**3. The decision trigger compares X to the wrong benchmark, and it will arrive late.**
- **Benchmark:** the decision is about X's share of the team's attempts. The relevant comparison is X against the teammates whose attempts he would take, not against the league's 36%. The expected-value paragraph already says this, so the trigger should say it too.
- **Timing:** at 4–5 attempts per game, 250–300 attempts is about 55–65 games, which is most of next season. Staff should know the trigger cannot fire early.

**4. Avoid suggesting he got worse.**
"6 points worse than before the change, not better" in Section 1 could be read that way. Section 2 correctly says 28% on 50 attempts is noise. The standard error of 28% vs 34% is about 7.4 points, so this difference is not meaningful either. Adding "(also within noise; see Section 2)" in Section 1 would keep readers from taking away the opposite wrong conclusion.

## Minor

- **Free throws:** they are only weakly related to three-point skill. "Reasonable, if imperfect" is fair. Don't give them more weight than that.
- **Team-level test:** the recommendation to check the team's own before-and-after split by opponent strength is the most useful next step. It could be moved higher in the report.

## Unchanged

The answer to both questions holds:

- There is no reliable evidence of genuine improvement.
- There is no case for increasing X's share of three-point attempts on these data.
